group.title: Work and jobs
sources: Words and CEFR levels chosen by the authors from general knowledge of English; meanings, examples and sentences are original

Word-list licences checked 2026-10-25: CEFR-J Wordlist 1.5 (Tono Laboratory, TUFS; free with citation, A1-B2) and NGSL/NAWL (CC BY-SA 4.0) were not copied; Oxford 3000 and English Vocabulary Profile terms were not confirmed, so they were not used

words.meaning: A group of people who make or sell things to earn money.
examples: My dad works for a big car {company}.
wrong: A company is a single person who works alone for free.

words.meaning: Buying and selling things to make money, or a company that does this.
examples: She has her own {business}, a small bakery.
wrong: His business is a hobby he never earns money from.

words.meaning: To stay at your job after the usual time.
examples: I have to {work late} tonight, so start dinner without me.
wrong: She worked late, so she left the office early at two.

words.meaning: All the people who work in a place.
examples: The hotel {staff} were very friendly.
wrong: The staff are the customers who visit the shop.

words.meaning: To record the time you start work.
examples: We {clock in} at eight with our cards at the door.
wrong: He clocked in when he went home at the end of the day.

words.meaning: The person something belongs to.
examples: The {owner} of the cafe also makes the cakes.
wrong: The owner of the shop is a customer who comes in once.

words.meaning: A business or company.
examples: She works for a law {firm} in the city.
wrong: A firm is a kind of hard chair.

words.meaning: For only some of the normal working hours.
examples: He has a {part-time} job on weekends.
wrong: Her part-time job is fifty hours a week.

words.meaning: For all of the normal working hours in a week.
examples: She has a {full-time} job, Monday to Friday.
wrong: He has a full-time job, two hours on Sundays.

words.meaning: To give someone a job and pay them.
examples: The hotel {employs} sixty people.
wrong: The shop employs ten people and pays none of them for any work.

words.meaning: To make someone leave their job.
examples: He was {fired} for being late every day.
wrong: They fired her, so she started her new job there.

words.meaning: To leave your job because you want to.
examples: She {quit} her job to travel the world.
wrong: He quit his job, so he goes there every day.

words.meaning: To get money for the work you do.
examples: She {earns} more money than her brother.
wrong: He earns money by paying other people.

words.meaning: A letter or form you send to ask for a job.
examples: I sent my {application} for the job last week.
wrong: An application is a thank-you card after you start a job.

words.meaning: A short rest from work to have a drink.
examples: Let’s have a {coffee break} at ten.
wrong: During my coffee break I work twice as hard without stopping.

words.meaning: The name of your job or position.
examples: Her {job title} is sales manager.
wrong: My job title is the money I earn each month.

words.meaning: Extra money added to your normal pay.
examples: Everyone got a {bonus} at the end of the year.
wrong: A bonus is money taken from your pay as a punishment.

words.meaning: The money you get for your work.
examples: The work is hard, but the {pay} is good.
wrong: The pay is the money you give your boss each month.

words.meaning: The day you get your money for work.
examples: {Payday} is the last Friday of the month.
wrong: On payday everyone gives money back to the company.

words.meaning: The money you get for work, often each week or month.
examples: Half of my {paycheck} goes on rent.
wrong: A paycheck is the bill you pay for food.

words.meaning: Giving a lot of money for the work.
examples: Doctors have {well-paid} jobs.
wrong: It’s a well-paid job, so he can’t buy food.

words.meaning: Having done a job for a long time and knowing it well.
examples: We need an {experienced} cook who has worked in hotels.
wrong: She is an experienced driver; today is her first time in a car.

words.meaning: Able to do a job well because of training.
examples: He is a {skilled} builder.
wrong: She is a skilled painter who can’t hold a brush.

words.meaning: A day when you go to work, or the hours you work that day.
examples: My {workday} starts at eight and ends at four.
wrong: Sunday is my workday, so I never work on it.

words.meaning: The times when an office is open.
examples: Please call during {office hours}, nine to five.
wrong: Office hours are the times when the office is closed.

words.meaning: A day you stay home from work because you are ill.
examples: I had a fever, so I took a {sick day}.
wrong: He took a sick day because he felt very well.

words.meaning: Not given any money for the work.
examples: She did {unpaid} work at the hospital to help.
wrong: It was an unpaid job, so she got a big check every week.

words.meaning: A time of work during the night.
examples: Nurses on the {night shift} work from ten until six.
wrong: He works the night shift, from nine in the morning to five.

words.meaning: The time of day when people are at work.
examples: My {working hours} are nine to five.
wrong: My working hours are the times I sleep at home.

words.meaning: A journey you make for your job.
examples: She is in Berlin on a {business trip} this week.
wrong: He went on a business trip to relax on the beach with his family.

words.meaning: The work of selling things, or the number of things sold.
examples: She works in {sales} and talks to customers all day.
wrong: Our sales went up because nobody bought anything.

words.meaning: A lot of effort to do something.
examples: The exam was easy for her after all her {hard work}.
wrong: Hard work means doing nothing all day.

words.meaning: To do your job at your house, not in an office.
examples: On Fridays I {work from home} and don’t take the bus.
wrong: I work from home, so I drive to the office every day.

words.meaning: Being the person who controls something or tells others what to do.
examples: Maria is {in charge of} the kitchen.
wrong: He is in charge of the team, so he does what everyone tells him.

words.meaning: Working at a certain time.
examples: Two police officers are {on duty} at the station tonight.
wrong: The guard was on duty, so he stayed home all night.

words.meaning: To start working for someone and getting paid.
examples: After school he {got a job} in a supermarket.
wrong: She got a job, so now she has no work at all.

words.meaning: To stop having work because your boss ends it.
examples: Many people {lost their jobs} when the factory closed.
wrong: He lost his job, so he goes to the same office every day.

words.meaning: To make the money you need to live.
examples: He {earns a living} as a taxi driver.
wrong: She earns a living by spending all her money.

words.meaning: To own and control a company.
examples: My aunt {runs a business} selling flowers.
wrong: He runs a business, but he has nothing to do with it.

words.meaning: At the place where you have your job.
examples: She’s {at work} until six, so call her later.
wrong: He is at work, at home in bed.
